findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and can be cancelled immediately
findings.body: Create derives its 10-second legacy-write context from the incoming request context; the same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Once the API handler finishes and returns the response, the request context is cancelled, so an in-flight legacy write can be aborted despite the 10-second timeout. This can silently leave legacy storage without the backup write that mode 3 is intended to provide. The context needs to be detached from request cancellation while preserving request values such as authentication.

findings.title: Async legacy Create races with use of the returned object
findings.body: Create passes the original obj to Legacy.Create in a goroutine after Storage.Create has returned created from that same input. Storage implementations may mutate obj or return an object aliasing it, while the caller will proceed to serialize or otherwise use created. The legacy store can therefore concurrently read or mutate shared object state, causing a data race or changing the response after unified storage has completed. The object should be deep-copied before launching the asynchronous legacy write.

findings.title: Update reuses objInfo instead of propagating the unified-storage result to legacy
findings.body: Update passes the same UpdatedObjectInfo independently to unified storage and then asynchronously to legacy storage, dropping the previous updateWrapper behavior. UpdatedObject will be computed a second time against legacy's old object, so the two stores can receive different content when their old objects or resource versions differ, and implementations that cache or mutate the decoded object can make the second computation incorrect. Legacy should receive the same updated object that unified storage accepted, as the previous implementation ensured.

findings.title: Storage failures are recorded in the wrong duration metric
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration; Update has the same mistake on its storage-error path, and DeleteCollection records its asynchronous legacy result with recordStorageDuration. Storage and legacy latency/error dashboards and alerts will therefore attribute failures to the wrong backend and can hide unified-storage errors.

findings.title: Delete uses the object name as the Prometheus kind label
findings.body: The successful Delete path calls recordStorageDuration with name where the other methods pass options.Kind. Prometheus labels must be bounded; using a distinct resource name for every deleted object creates unbounded metric cardinality, increasing memory and query cost and breaking comparisons by kind. It should pass options.Kind like the error path and other methods.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: Mode 3 launches fire-and-forget goroutines for legacy writes but keeps no WaitGroup or other tracking. Destroy immediately destroys both storages, so shutdown can terminate or close legacy storage while writes are still running, losing backup writes or causing use-after-destroy failures. Asynchronous work needs to be tracked and drained before the underlying storages are destroyed.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: The new tests invoke Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection but do not wait for or assert the legacy goroutines, and both stores share one testify mock with indistinguishable expectations. The tests therefore pass even if a legacy method is never called, is called with the wrong object, or fails asynchronously after the test returns. They need synchronization and separate assertions that each legacy operation eventually runs with the expected arguments.

findings.title: Mode 3 playlist integration test assumes synchronous legacy visibility
findings.body: The new mode 3 integration cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates or updates through the Kubernetes API and immediately reads the same data through the legacy playlist API. Mode 3 now writes to legacy in a background goroutine, so there is no ordering guarantee that the legacy rows exist when those immediate assertions run. This introduces intermittent integration-test failures unless the test polls for legacy visibility or the helper waits for asynchronous writes to settle.
